reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that publishability depends on sufficient sample size n, forming a constraint on probabilistic inference. The shadow diagnostic refusal introduces an early warning system where a single diagnostic signal can prevent publication. Categorical leverage allows for decision-making even when probabilities are not available. These form a triadic structure: (1) validity gate (n), (2) safety gate (diagnostic), and (3) utility gate (category). Each primitive operates in a distinct regime—probabilistic, diagnostic, and categorical—and together they define a robust inference pipeline. Failure modes include over-reliance on n alone, ignoring diagnostic warnings, or misclassifying categorical data. Dualities emerge between probabilistic and categorical reasoning, where each can substitute for the other under certain conditions.
